prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate that nearly the whole committee ranked: seven of eight members placed B037 on their ballot, two first, four in the top three. On the merits it is a clean instrument-and-measurement achievement. Katori's magic-wavelength idea made it possible to trap many atoms without shifting the clock transition, and his strontium demonstration made the concept real. Ye's group then drove systematic uncertainty to about 1e-18 and into the many-body regime. Several independent laboratories now operate lattice clocks, intercompare them and agree, and this feeds directly into the coming redefinition of the second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. The credit is two names, with a clear division between the proposer and first demonstrator and the group that brought it to the accuracy frontier. That is as clean as any attribution on this list. It is a result a detector builder trusts because it rests on calibration, systematics and independent confirmation rather than on a single claim. As Chair I would rather build the prize on the candidate with the broadest real support than on my own first choice.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with prior recognition in the same neighbourhood: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb, the 2012 prize for ion control and the 1997 and 2001 laser-cooling prizes. A sceptic can call lattice clocks an incremental, if spectacular, refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new discovery of nature. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the case is prospective. Ion clocks (Al+ and others) reach comparable uncertainty and their originators are outside this credit, so a two-name prize could be seen as unfair to that community. I am an astroparticle physicist, not an atomic physicist, and I cannot settle that relative-merit question myself.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a measurement advance with an unambiguous invention and a clean two-laureate credit, while noting overlap with the 2012 prize and the open question of a third name.
responses.response: I agree with the core argument and the two-name structure. I do not think the 2012 overlap is disqualifying. Wineland's prize was for isolating and controlling single quantum systems, and the lattice clock's contribution is different: interrogating a large ensemble at the magic wavelength so that statistics and systematics improve together. I would still want the committee to ask the atomic physicists to confirm that statement formally. Your caution about a third name is right. I see no clear candidate for one in the supplied credit, and padding to three would weaken the citation.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B037 first for its close theory-experiment agreement, with independent labs, redefinition of the second under discussion, and the open question of ion clocks and the priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal.
responses.response: Your point about the priority history is the one I most want checked, because everything else about attribution depends on it. Katori's proposal and early strontium work and the JILA record-setting work should be separable in an expert report. I would qualify one thing: the redefinition of the second is a strong argument for timeliness but a poor argument for merit, and we should keep the citation about the invention and its demonstrated accuracy, not the redefinition that has not yet happened.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first, as the experimental completion of the electroweak sector that the 2013 prize did not recognise, while admitting credit among thousands of collaborators is a compromise.
responses.response: I ranked B006 fourth and I respect the argument that the experimental discovery is unrecognised. But I disagree that this is simply overdue. Spokespersons and founding leaders are the weakest kind of credit: the discovery rests on the analyses, the trigger, the calorimeters and the tracker, and the LHC itself, and the three names stand in for thousands. Having built detectors in collaborations, I do not think leadership alone is the decisive contribution under the statute. I would keep B006 as an alternative, but only if we find a defensible attribution, which I have not yet seen.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for its tight prediction and measurement link and second the topological insulator entry, but notes the superconducting mechanism is unresolved and credit for the lead student and earlier twist theory is outside the names.
responses.response: I find the prediction-then-experiment chain in B018 persuasive, but I weigh the unresolved mechanism and the early date more heavily than you do. Reproduction across many labs confirms the phenomenon; it does not yet tell me what the prize would be for, beyond the platform. B042 is the stronger of your two for maturity, and I would take it as my first alternative. My concern there, which you also raised, is the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit and the overlap with the 2016 prize. I would defer to you and Bernhard on whether the three named people give a fair reading.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, as the foundational step that made superconducting circuits controllable quantum systems, complementary to the 2025 prize, and discloses his proximity to the community.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure and I accept that circuit QED is mature and not subsumed by the 2025 award. My difficulty is timing and platform. Having just recognised superconducting circuits, a second prize in that vicinity is hard to justify next to candidates that have not been honoured. The credit also leaves out Girvin, who co-authored the proposal, which you flagged yourself. I would not oppose B008 on merit, but I do not see it overtaking B037 on breadth of support.

uncertainties: Priority and relative decisiveness of the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock, and the later accuracy work, which should be checked by atomic-physics colleagues or an expert review.
Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether ion-clock originators would be seen as unfairly excluded.
Whether a single-achievement prize or a two-achievement prize is wiser, since my own first choice B003 has little support and a second part would force an awkward split of the three-person cap.
My own first-ranked candidate B003 has uncertain attribution among BeppoSAX, optical and radio follow-up teams, including deceased contributors.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B037, B042, B006 or B008. For B003 (gamma-ray burst afterglows) I have a general field affinity as a high-energy astrophysics instrument builder and my work involves Fermi-LAT, which is related to the field, but no personal or institutional tie to Costa, Frontera or Kulkarni. For B006 I have a general particle-physics background from my PhD at CERN but no direct tie to ATLAS or CMS.
